These trips would spark the idea that laid the foundation for what would become the first Glymph Family Reunion. Unfortunately, Al passed away before seeing the fruits of his labor when the inaugural Glymph Family Reunion was held back at the home place in Newberry, SC in 1980. There was participation by both the young and old, near and far. Stories were shared and the experiences that brought us all together were evidenced that weekend. The family voted to continue the tradition and agreed to rotate the host location to cities in which large numbers of family resided. Family members from the host site formed committees to orchestrate the much anticipated reunions and ensure that the reunions continued. chunks.text: GLYMPH’S! Frank Glymph was 100% Nigerian. He was born into and freed from slavery in Newberry, South Carolina, where he met and married Lide. Five children were born from this union. They were Henrietta, Laura Ann, Drucilla, Edward George and Carrie Glymph. In addition, Frank and Lide raised their grandson Frank “Tack” Chaplin Glymph Edward George was the only son of Frank and Lide. When E. George came of age, he married Minnie Lyles Richardson, and they were blessed with three sons: Ulysses, Clarence, and George. Minnie died shortly after the birth of her last son and E. George later married Sarah Ann Richardson, Minnie’s sister. E George was a farmer and in 1908 he purchased 59 acres of land in Newberry County where he raised his sons and grandchildren. Ulysses Glymph, who was the oldest, worked as a farmer for many years in Newberry County. In later years he operated a sawmill. He soon took up with his wife Mattie Ruff and they had 10 children Minnie, James, Asberry, George, Ulysses, Lily Mae, Heyward, Johnny, Woodrow and Pounee. Clarence

chunks.text: Glymph, the second oldest son, married Dolly Ruff and they were blessed with seven children Bertha Lee, Claudia, Blanche, Beatrice, Clarence, Jr, Thomas and Dolly. He left Newberry County in 1920 where he settled in Gaffney, South Carolina to become a prominent businessman and civic leader. George Glymph, although the youngest son was the first to move to Gaffney and he invites his brother Clarence to join him after receiving his dentistry degree at Meharry Medical College. George became a dentist and later established his practice in Spartanburg South Carolina. He married Vivian Cottingham, and they had four children, Mildred, Harold, Helen, and George Jr. The fruit that Frank and Lide produced is alive and well. today the Glymph Family is spread throughout the United States. You can find someone from the Glymph Family Tree mastering any profession imaginable. We have become doctors, lawyers, government workers, politicians, teachers, engineers, first responders, factory workers, authors, media professions, business professionals, and business owners. We also have many college students, retirees and babies which keep our fruit alive. You name it and we’re

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: doing it. This is not about us being boastful. It’s just mere facts. If Frank and Lide were alive today, they would certainly be bragging about their family. Look at what we have given to this world. From the days they lived in Newberry, SC, born into slavery, they surely couldn’t have imagined their descendants branching out this far and wide. The unity, strength, honor and will of this family speaks for itself. But, as we all know, none of us will mind telling you... “WE ARE GLYMPHS!!!” 14 History GLYMPH FAMILY GLYMPH FAMILY This year, the Glymph family celebrates its 21st family reunion. Spanning over forty- five years and ten states this rich tradition has grown into much more than a family cookout. In the late 1970s Asberry “A.B.” Glymph, out of the love for his family and commitment to ensure that his children, nieces and nephews grew to know and love one another, planned family trips that would take his brothers and sisters and their families to Virginia Beach, Virginia and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina. These trips would

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: spark the idea that laid the foundation for what would become the first Glymph family reunion. Unfortunately, A.B. passed away before seeing the fruits of his labor when the inaugural Glymph family reunion was held back at the “Home” place in Newberry, South Carolina in 1980. There was participation by both the young and old, near and far. Stories were shared, and the experiences that brought us all together were evidenced that weekend. The family voted to continue the tradition and agreed to rotate the host location to cities in which large numbers of families resided. Family members from the host site formed committees to orchestrate the much-anticipated reunion and ensure that the reunions continued. Our gatherings took us to Cleveland, Ohio in 1981, Rochelle Park, New Jersey in 1983, Newberry, South Carolina in 1987, Detroit, Michigan in 1989, Cleveland, Ohio in 1991, and back to Newberry South Carolina in 1994, at which the torch was passed down to the next generation who took the lead and planned their first reunion in 1996 in Virginia Beach, Virginia. Reunions continued in

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: Detroit, Michigan in 2000, Atlanta, Georgia in 2002 and Cleveland, Ohio in 2004. Wanting to keep the reunions fresh and to incorporate the ideas of more family members, the family embraced the use of technology to coordinate destination reunions by reconstructing the committee format to include representatives from various states. The reunions continued to flourish, participation grew and yielded additional outreach for Glymph’s to become involved. Destination reunions have taken us to Myrtle Beach, South Carolina in 2006 and Pigeon Forge, Tennessee in 2008, we returned to the home place of Newberry, South Carolina in 2010, Ocean City, Maryland in 2012, Wilmington, North Carolina in 2014, Cleveland, Ohio in 2016, and Savannah, Georgia in 2018. The 2020 reunion that was scheduled to take place in Columbia, South Carolina underwent a remarkable transformation due to the COVID-19 pandemic. We yearned for the cherished physical togetherness, yet fate dictated a virtual reunion for the Glymph family. This unprecedented circumstance created an opportunity to utilize the power of technology, linking our dispersed clans, as well as welcoming new families into our embrace, scattered

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: across the nation. As we emerged from the global crisis, we confronted an ever-changing world evolving before our eyes for our 20th reunion. This reunion is taking us back to a state that we have previously hosted. We made such joyous memories in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee that this time we visit Nashville for new ones.. While each reunion has certainly been different, all have offered the perfect platform to learn more about the rich Glymph history, reconnect with family, enjoy the offerings of the host city and most importantly always remember...We are GLYMPH’S....we are nine-generations strong. We all we got! 15 Reunion History 16 WELCOMING ANDREW’S BRANCH WELCOMING ANDREW’S BRANCH Frank's Brother Andrew’s branch A Brotherhood Reunited Through DNA In 2023, for the first time, we learned through DNA testing something remarkable: Frank had a older brother—Andrew. Born in 1827, Andrew’s existence had never been part of

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: the known family story. No one alive today could say how he ended up in Arkansas, while Frank remained in South Carolina. But the discovery shed light on a bond that had long been lost to history, buried by time and the cruel displacements caused by slavery. We can only imagine what happened after the two brothers were freed. Perhaps Andrew, still young, chose to leave, searching for an opportunity or simply a new beginning. Somehow, he found his way to Arkansas, where his branch of the family tree took root—separated from Frank’s, but never severed. Back in 1986, decades before DNA could connect people across generations, Linda, her mother, grandmother, and four others made a journey to South Carolina. They came looking for family. They had always heard that their people were from South Carolina, but they didn’t have names or concrete connections—only stories and instincts passed down through generations. While there, they met James A. Glymph, George Glymph, and Walter Glymph. The men welcomed them with warmth and curiosity. Though they couldn’t pinpoint the exact relationship at the

chunks.title: Glymph-Family-Reunion-Book-2025-1
chunks.text: time, they believed there had to be a connection. They showed Linda’s family around, shared what they knew, and kept the door open. That trip planted a seed. Over the years, the rise of DNA technology revolutionized how families—especially Black families separated during slavery—could reconnect. What oral history couldn’t confirm, DNA could begin to trace. And little by little, Frank’s bloodline began appearing within Andrew’s. Distant cousins, shared genetic markers, overlapping trees. What once was speculation became fact: Frank and Andrew were brothers. This discovery was more than just a scientific match—it was a restoration of lost family. It brought clarity to the stories Linda’s family had always held onto. It confirmed the hunches of the Glymph’s back in 1986. It gave two fractured branches of a family a shared beginning. Their union was blessed with two sons, Sean and Brent Thomas, to whom she devoted her life. Her passion for nurturing children extended beyond her own home — Johnnie began her career in education as a preschool teacher and was part of one of the first Head Start programs in Cleveland. In 1968, the Thomas

After spending five years as a stay-at-home mother, she joined Southfield Public Schools as a paraprofessional. Over a dedicated 31-year career, she made a lasting impact on students and staff alike. As her sons attended school in Southfield, Johnnie was an ever-present and active parent — participating in the PTA and serving on numerous parent-led committees. Her unwavering support and involvement were pivotal in her sons' academic journeys. Tragedy struck in 1986 when Johnnie lost her husband James to cancer. With courage and the support of her family, she took on the role of both parents, never wavering in her commitment to her sons. Faith and community were guiding forces in Johnnie’s life. Influenced by her mother’s example, she became deeply involved in

She remains active, enjoying regular outings with her "Birthday Crew," a group of lifelong friends and former colleagues. Proud of her Black heritage, Johnnie has passed down this pride and strength to her sons and her heart and soul — her granddaughter, Brielle. Her legacy is one of service, strength, and love — a life beautifully lived and still inspiring others. GLYMPH FAMILY GLYMPH FAMILY Matriarch JOHNNIE MAE GLYMPH THOMAS cont... Many have asked where Robert got his nickname “Socrates.” It was Dr. and Mrs. Moore who gave him the nickname, and the family kept it going by affectionately calling him “Soc.” People he grew up with still call him by that name today. Robert’s parents’ stay in the Biltmore Estates community was short-lived when his father chose to relocate to the North to find work in Ohio. Robert grew up in the Cleveland Metropolitan Housing Projects, but as a child, he loved spending summers down South visiting family. He attended Shiloh Baptist Church and was baptized on May 22, 1955. During high school, he worked at Huron Road Hospital and later joined his Uncle Woodrow Glymph at the Excel Cellophane Company. That job eventually afforded him his first car—a yellow and white Ford Fairlane. Many of his friends labeled him “Cool Bob” after that purchase. Robert graduated from East Technical High School on June 15, 1959, and married his wife, Juanita, a few years later on August 12, 1962. He
